z-m-08-01.title: Minjae's calculation table for the number of pages in 23 books
z-m-08-01.topic: Place value in multiplying a three-digit number by a two-digit number
z-m-08-01.goal: Find the line in a column-multiplication table where the place value went wrong, check the answer by estimating and by using the last digit, and then rewrite it correctly.
z-m-08-01.material: At the library, 23 storybooks of 346 pages each were bought. Minjae used column multiplication to find the total number of pages. There is no picture, so Minjae's calculation table is written out in words, line by line.
z-m-08-01.thinking.0: Finding where the error is in the calculation
z-m-08-01.thinking.1: Checking the result by estimating and by using the last digit
z-m-08-01.thinking.2: Explaining the corrected calculation and the reason
z-m-08-01.prereq.0: Reading a column-multiplication table and telling the values of the ones, tens, and hundreds places (Grade 4 level)
z-m-08-01.prereq.1: Comparing the size of a calculation result with an estimated value
z-m-08-01.s.s1.prompt: Choose the first line in Minjae's calculation table that goes wrong.
z-m-08-01.s.s1.hint.0: For each line, write in words what value the multiplier has (which place the digit 2 is in).
z-m-08-01.s.s1.hint.1: Estimate roughly how many pages 20 books of 346 pages would be, and compare it with 1730.
z-m-08-01.s.s1.line.0: Write 23 under 346, and start multiplying with the 3 in the ones place.
z-m-08-01.s.s1.line.1: Write 346 × 3 = 1038, lined up from the ones place.
z-m-08-01.s.s1.line.2: Multiply by the 2 in the tens place too. Write 346 × 2 = 692, with its right end lined up directly under 1038.
z-m-08-01.s.s1.line.4: So the 23 books have 1730 pages in all.
z-m-08-01.s.s1.explain: It first went wrong on line 3. The 2 in 23 is in the tens place, so it means 20, not 2. So 346 × 2 = 692 must be written one place to the left (692 must be read as 6920). The addition on line 4, 1038 + 692 = 1730, is correct by itself, but the two numbers being added are wrong, and the answer on line 5 is the result of that.
z-m-08-01.s.s2.prompt: Choose all the reasons that let you tell that 1730 pages is wrong without finishing the calculation.
z-m-08-01.s.s2.hint.0: First estimate roughly how many times the pages of one book the 23 books have.
z-m-08-01.s.s2.hint.1: Without calculating, decide whether each choice is true or false, then check whether the true choices contradict 1730.
z-m-08-01.s.s2.o.a: 346 is more than 300 and 23 is more than 20, so the product must be more than 6000
z-m-08-01.s.s2.r.a: Estimating the size first is a good habit.
z-m-08-01.s.s2.o.b: 346 and 23 are both even, so the product must be even, but 1730 is odd
z-m-08-01.s.s2.r.b: 23 is odd and 1730 is even. When you talk about even and odd, first check exactly which two numbers are being multiplied.
z-m-08-01.s.s2.o.c: Since 6 × 3 = 18, the ones digit of the product must be 8, but 1730 ends in 0
z-m-08-01.s.s2.r.c: Multiplying the ones digits to check the last digit is a good check too.
z-m-08-01.s.s2.o.d: Since 692 is less than 1038, the sum 1730 must be less than 1038
z-m-08-01.s.s2.r.d: Adding two numbers makes a result bigger than either one. Look again at how to compare a sum with one of the two numbers.
z-m-08-01.s.s2.o.e: Each book has 346 pages and there are 23 books, so the answer must be more than 346, and 1730 is more than 346
z-m-08-01.s.s2.r.e: It is true that 1730 is more than 346. But that alone does not show that 1730 is wrong. You need to estimate a more fitting size.
z-m-08-01.s.s2.explain: Estimating 300 × 20 = 6000, the answer must be more than 6000 pages, and from multiplying the ones digits, 6 × 3 = 18, the last digit must be 8. Neither reason fits 1730. The even/odd reason (b) is wrong because 23 is odd, and d and e are not evidence that 1730 is wrong.
z-m-08-01.s.s3.prompt: Rewrite Minjae's calculation table and find the correct number of pages. Also write in your own words why the line you changed has to be changed that way.
z-m-08-01.s.s3.hint.0: First write down what value the digit 2 in the tens place stands for.
z-m-08-01.s.s3.hint.1: Write the results of 346 × 2 and 346 × 20 side by side, and compare which one belongs in the correct line.
z-m-08-01.s.s3.placeholder: e.g., The 2 in the tens place is ...
z-m-08-01.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you write why the number multiplied with 346 in your corrected calculation is 20 (or a value like 6920) instead of 2?
z-m-08-01.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you check, by estimating or by using the last digit, that the method you used (adding a 0, shifting one place to the left, multiplying by 20) agrees with 7958 pages?
z-m-08-01.s.s3.model.0: 346 × 20 = 6920. The 2 in the tens place is 20, so you have to write 6920, not 692. 1038 + 6920 = 7958 pages.
z-m-08-01.s.s3.model.1: Shift 692 one place to the left. When you multiply by the digit in the tens place, the ones place is empty, so you have to think of it as having a 0 there. 1038 + 6920 = 7958, so it is 7958 pages.

z-m-08-02.title: Two cards that add up to 90: will the scores be the same too?
z-m-08-02.topic: Comparing the sizes of products of two two-digit numbers
z-m-08-02.goal: Understand that one example cannot confirm "always the same", make different examples that meet the condition, compare them, and describe what pairs with bigger scores have in common.
z-m-08-02.material: Let's play a number card game. Each card has one natural number from 10 to 99 written on it. Rule: you pick two cards, and the two numbers must add up to exactly 90. The score is the two numbers multiplied together. Sua picked 40 and 50 and got 2000 points. Then she said, "If the sum is 90, the score is always 2000 points!" The order you place the cards in doesn't matter. (30 and 60, and 60 and 30, are the same pair.)
z-m-08-02.thinking.0: Telling apart what one example does and does not tell you
z-m-08-02.thinking.1: Making several examples within the condition
z-m-08-02.thinking.2: Comparing the examples and guessing the rule
z-m-08-02.prereq.0: Multiplying two-digit numbers by each other (Grade 4 level, without a calculator)
z-m-08-02.prereq.1: Pairing natural numbers so they have the same sum
z-m-08-02.s.s1.prompt: Sua spoke after seeing the result of the one pair 40 and 50. What does the result of this one pair tell us about Sua's statement?
z-m-08-02.s.s1.hint.0: Sua's statement includes the word "always". Think of the quickest action to find out whether that statement is true.
z-m-08-02.s.s1.hint.1: Make any one more pair with a sum of 90 and find its score.
z-m-08-02.s.s1.o.a: 40 and 50 gave 2000 points, so any pair gives 2000 points
z-m-08-02.s.s1.r.a: One example being right does not prove "always". How about testing other pairs too?
z-m-08-02.s.s1.o.b: It can't be decided until we check another pair with a sum of 90
z-m-08-02.s.s1.r.b: You pointed out that one example alone can't tell us "always".
z-m-08-02.s.s1.o.c: We can decide right now that the scores are not the same even when the sums are the same
z-m-08-02.s.s1.r.c: The result of one pair alone cannot confirm "not the same". You have to actually make other pairs and compare.
z-m-08-02.s.s1.o.d: We don't know yet. So we don't need to check any other pair
z-m-08-02.s.s1.r.d: You're right to feel that you don't know, but when you don't know, testing is the next step.
z-m-08-02.s.s1.explain: 40 and 50 giving 2000 points is just one example that doesn't contradict Sua's statement. To know whether "if the sum is 90, the score is always the same" is true, you have to check other pairs with a sum of 90. If another pair gives a different score, that pair is a counterexample.
z-m-08-02.s.s2.prompt: Make three pairs of two-digit cards with a sum of 90 that have different scores. (Swapping the two cards gives the same pair.)
z-m-08-02.s.s2.hint.0: Pick the first card, then subtract that number from 90 to make the second card.
z-m-08-02.s.s2.hint.1: Change the first card, skipping from 10 up to 90, but check that both numbers are two-digit numbers.
z-m-08-02.s.s2.fail.c1: The cards have only natural numbers written on them.
z-m-08-02.s.s2.fail.c2: The numbers on the cards are two-digit numbers from 10 to 99.
z-m-08-02.s.s2.ok.c3: The sum of the two numbers is 90.
z-m-08-02.s.s2.fail.c3: The sum of the two numbers is not 90. Add them to check.
z-m-08-02.s.s2.explain: Pairs with a sum of 90 have different scores, such as (40, 50) = 2000 points, (30, 60) = 1800 points, (20, 70) = 1400 points, (45, 45) = 2025 points, and (11, 79) = 869 points. Since some pairs have the same sum but different products, Sua's statement is not always true. A swapped pair (50 and 40) is the same pair, so count it as only one.
z-m-08-02.s.s3.prompt: Compare the scores of the pairs you made. What did the two numbers look like in the pair with the biggest score? Describe one way to pick cards so that the score gets bigger. Use pairs you actually found as examples.
z-m-08-02.s.s3.hint.0: Write the scores of the pairs you made in order from biggest to smallest, and also write the difference between the two numbers in each pair.
z-m-08-02.s.s3.hint.1: Compare how far apart the two numbers are in the pairs with big scores and in the pairs with small scores.
z-m-08-02.s.s3.placeholder: e.g., The pair with the biggest score was ...
z-m-08-02.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you actually multiply to find the scores of your examples?
z-m-08-02.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Can you test one more time whether a new pair picked by the method you described really gets a bigger score?
z-m-08-02.s.s3.model.0: 40 and 50 gave 2000 points, 30 and 60 gave 1800 points, and 20 and 70 gave 1400 points. The closer the two numbers were, the bigger the score. So if I pick numbers with a small difference like 45 and 45, I think it will be even bigger.
z-m-08-02.s.s3.model.1: The smaller the difference in the pair, the bigger the score. The difference between 40 and 50 is 10 and the score is 2000, but 20 and 70 have a difference of 50 and give 1400. When the sum is 90, it's good to pick numbers close to 45.

z-m-08-03.title: Packing 14 to a box so that the leftover pieces are an odd number
z-m-08-03.topic: The relationship between the quotient and the remainder in division
z-m-08-03.goal: Learn the range of values the leftover can take, make different examples of the dividend, quotient, and leftover that meet the conditions, and explain why the range is what it is.
z-m-08-03.material: A chocolate factory packs exactly 14 chocolates in each box. Only full boxes are counted, and the loose pieces that can't fill a box are not put in a box but set aside. Call the number of chocolates made a, the number of full boxes q, and the number of loose pieces set aside r. (a is between 100 and 999.)
z-m-08-03.thinking.0: Telling possible cases from impossible cases
z-m-08-03.thinking.1: Making examples that meet several conditions at once
z-m-08-03.prereq.1: Knowing the relationship divisor × quotient + remainder = dividend
z-m-08-03.s.s1.prompt: Chocolates are packed 14 to a box, and there is at least 1 loose piece left over. Choose all the numbers that the number of loose pieces r can be.
z-m-08-03.s.s1.hint.0: Think about what you could do with the leftover pieces when 14 pieces are left.
z-m-08-03.s.s1.hint.1: For each choice, check one by one whether the leftover pieces could fill one more box.
z-m-08-03.s.s1.r.a: If 14 pieces are left, you can put those 14 in one box. What happens to the number of boxes then?
z-m-08-03.s.s1.r.b: You thought of the case where fewer than 14 pieces are left.
z-m-08-03.s.s1.r.c: If 17 pieces are left, you can fill one more box. How many are left then? Think again about how many can be left at most.
z-m-08-03.s.s1.r.d: This is the case where exactly one piece is missing to fill a box.
z-m-08-03.s.s1.r.e: If 28 pieces are left, you can fill two more boxes. Think again about the range of the leftover.
z-m-08-03.s.s1.r.f: You found the case where fewer than 14 are left.
z-m-08-03.s.s1.explain: Only full boxes are counted, so if 14 or more loose pieces are left, you can fill more boxes. So the leftover can only be from 1 to 13. 5, 13, and 9 are possible, and 14, 17, and 28 are not.
z-m-08-03.s.s2.prompt: Make three different cases where the number of chocolates a, the number of full boxes q, and the number of loose pieces r all follow these conditions. Conditions: the number of boxes is 10 or more and 99 or fewer, and the number of loose pieces is odd.
z-m-08-03.s.s2.hint.0: Decide the number of boxes q first, then find how many chocolates are packed in q boxes of 14.
z-m-08-03.s.s2.hint.1: Add an odd number of loose pieces to that to make a, then check that the loose pieces are fewer than 14.
z-m-08-03.s.s2.ok.c1: All three numbers are natural numbers.
z-m-08-03.s.s2.fail.c1: The counts must be natural numbers.
z-m-08-03.s.s2.ok.c2: The number of chocolates is between 100 and 999.
z-m-08-03.s.s2.fail.c2: The number of chocolates made must be between 100 and 999.
z-m-08-03.s.s2.ok.c3: The number of boxes is 10 or more and 99 or fewer.
z-m-08-03.s.s2.fail.c3: The number of full boxes must be 10 or more and 99 or fewer.
z-m-08-03.s.s2.ok.c4: The chocolates packed in boxes plus the loose pieces equal the number of chocolates made.
z-m-08-03.s.s2.fail.c4: Add the chocolates in the boxes of 14 and the loose pieces, and check whether the total equals a.
z-m-08-03.s.s2.ok.c5: The number of loose pieces is fewer than 14.
z-m-08-03.s.s2.fail.c5: If 14 or more loose pieces are left, you can fill more boxes. The loose pieces left must be fewer than 14.
z-m-08-03.s.s2.ok.c6: The number of loose pieces is odd.
z-m-08-03.s.s2.fail.c6: The number of loose pieces is not odd.
z-m-08-03.s.s2.explain: For example, 14 × 12 + 5 = 173, so 173 chocolates fill 12 boxes with 5 loose pieces left over. 14 × 25 + 9 = 359, 14 × 40 + 13 = 573, and 14 × 71 + 1 = 995 also fit the conditions. If you write 188 chocolates as 12 boxes and 20 loose pieces, the sum is right, but it is wrong because the 20 loose pieces can fill one more box.
z-m-08-03.s.s2.because.prompt: Why does the number of loose pieces r have to be fewer than 14? Write the reason in your own words.
z-m-08-03.s.s2.because.hint.0: Write down what you could do with the leftover pieces when r is 14, 15, and 20, one by one.
z-m-08-03.s.s2.because.hint.1: Write down how q and r change after you do that.
z-m-08-03.s.s2.because.placeholder: e.g., If 14 or more are left, ...
z-m-08-03.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Is your reason connected to what happens when 14 or more are left (filling more boxes)?
z-m-08-03.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did you check that r is less than 14 in all three of your examples?
z-m-08-03.s.s2.because.model.0: If 14 or more loose pieces are left, you can fill one more box. Then the number of boxes goes up by one and the leftover goes down. So the leftover has to be fewer than 14.
z-m-08-03.s.s2.because.model.1: It's what's left after taking out groups of 14, so if more than 14 are left, you can take out another group. The number left when you can't take out any more is the remainder, so it is less than 14.

z-m-08-04.title: High jump records: who jumped higher?
z-m-08-04.topic: Comparing a one-decimal-place number with a three-decimal-place number
z-m-08-04.goal: Compare decimals by place value instead of by how many digits they have, check your judgment as new data comes in, and make your own counterexample to a wrong rule.
z-m-08-04.material: At the school sports day high jump, Seoyun's and Dohyeon's records were measured. A record is the height in meters (m) from the floor to the bar, measured with a tape measure. The records are given to you one step at a time.
z-m-08-04.thinking.0: Checking your judgment as data is added
z-m-08-04.thinking.1: Comparing sizes of decimals by place value
z-m-08-04.s.s1.prompt: Look at the data one piece at a time, judge who jumped higher, and check your judgment when new data comes in.
z-m-08-04.s.s1.hint.0: At each step, judge using only what you know so far, and first write in words whether your judgment changes when new data comes in.
z-m-08-04.s.s1.hint.1: Change the two records to the same unit and compare them side by side.
z-m-08-04.s.s1.st.0.info: Seoyun's record is 1.4 m and Dohyeon's record is 1.38 m.
z-m-08-04.s.s1.st.0.ask: Looking only at the digits, what do you think right now?
z-m-08-04.s.s1.st.0.after: Both the judgment that Seoyun is higher and the judgment that it is too early to decide are reasonable at this step. You can decide by first comparing the tenths places.
z-m-08-04.s.s1.st.0.r.a: This may be a judgment that looked at the place values of the tenths and hundredths places.
z-m-08-04.s.s1.st.0.o.b: Dohyeon jumped higher, because 38 is bigger than 4
z-m-08-04.s.s1.st.0.r.b: You read the digits after the decimal point like a whole number and compared 38 and 4. With decimals, you must first look at which place each digit is in.
z-m-08-04.s.s1.st.0.o.c: It's hard to decide from the digits alone
z-m-08-04.s.s1.st.0.r.c: Honestly admitting that you're not sure and waiting for the next data is reasonable too.
z-m-08-04.s.s1.st.1.ask: Now that you've seen the scale data, who do you think is higher?
z-m-08-04.s.s1.st.1.after: 1.4 m is the same as 1.40 m, so it is 40 sections. Even with fewer digits, a number can be bigger because of place value.
z-m-08-04.s.s1.st.1.r.a: On the 100-section scale, 1.4 is 40 sections, so it is above 38 sections.
z-m-08-04.s.s1.st.1.r.b: Check again on the scale that the number 38 is less than 40.
z-m-08-04.s.s1.st.1.r.c: Both records are on the scale, so you can decide with this data.
z-m-08-04.s.s1.st.2.info: Harin jumped too. Harin's record is 1.405 m. And Seoyun's 1.4 m is the same height whether you write it as 1.40 m or 1.400 m.
z-m-08-04.s.s1.st.2.ask: Which one lists the three records in order from highest to lowest?
z-m-08-04.s.s1.st.2.after: 1.405 is 0.005 higher than 1.400. So the order is Harin, Seoyun, Dohyeon. The order of Seoyun and Dohyeon did not change when the new data came in.
z-m-08-04.s.s1.st.2.r.a: This is the order you get by thinking that the one with more digits is bigger. Write 1.4 as 1.400 and compare starting from the tenths place.
z-m-08-04.s.s1.st.2.r.b: 1.405 and 1.4 (= 1.400) first differ in the thousandths place, and 1.38 differs in the hundredths place.
z-m-08-04.s.s1.st.2.o.c: Seoyun and Harin are the same, and Dohyeon is the lowest
z-m-08-04.s.s1.st.2.r.c: You ignored the 5 at the end of 1.405. 1.400 and 1.405 are different numbers.
z-m-08-04.s.s1.reflect: Even when new data came in, the judgment that Seoyun jumped higher than Dohyeon stayed the same. What changed was the order after Harin was added. Decimals are compared by the place value of each digit, not by how many digits there are.
z-m-08-04.s.s2.hint.0: Think of two decimals whose tenths digits are different.
z-m-08-04.s.s2.hint.1: Write the bigger number out to the hundredths place (with a 0 attached) and compare the two numbers side by side.
z-m-08-04.s.s2.selfAssess.0: In the two decimals you gave, is the one with more digits the smaller number?
z-m-08-04.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you think about the fact that the same height can be written with a different number of digits after the decimal point (1.4 = 1.40)?
z-m-08-04.s.s2.model.0: Look at 0.5 and 0.45. 0.45 has more digits, but 0.5 is 0.50, so it is bigger than 0.45.

z-m-08-05.title: The length left after using 3.47 m from a 10 m ribbon
z-m-08-05.topic: Comparing ways to subtract a two-decimal-place number from a whole number
z-m-08-05.goal: Compare several ways of solving the same problem to pick out the correct ones, use estimation to filter out wrong answers, and say which method suits these particular numbers, with a reason.
z-m-08-05.material:
From a ribbon 10 m long, 3.47 m was cut off and used. Five friends found the length of the remaining ribbon like this.
Mina: Subtract 3 from 10 to get 7, then attach the decimal part 0.47 as it is, so 7.47 m.
Jiho: Write 10 as 10.00, line up the decimal points, and subtract vertically to get 6.53 m.
Haneul: Change 3.47 to 3.5 and subtract to get exactly 6.5 m.
Raon: See 10 as 1000/100 and 3.47 as 347/100 to get 653/100, which is 6.53 m.
Soyeon: Subtract 3 from 10 to make 7, then subtract 0.47 more from 7 to get 6.53 m.
z-m-08-05.thinking.1: Checking whether an answer is reasonable by estimating
z-m-08-05.thinking.2: Comparing methods, choosing one, and saying when it fits
z-m-08-05.prereq.0: Meaning of a two-decimal-place number and lining up the decimal points
z-m-08-05.prereq.1: The relationship between fractions with denominator 100 and decimals (Grade 4 level)
z-m-08-05.s.s1.prompt: Choose all the methods that correctly find the exact length of the remaining ribbon.
z-m-08-05.s.s1.hint.0: Follow each friend's method and write down what happens to 3.47 while subtracting it from 10.
z-m-08-05.s.s1.hint.1: Check whether a method that claims an exact value changed or left out any number.
z-m-08-05.s.s1.r.a: If you attach the decimal part as it is, you have only subtracted the 3 from 3.47. Look again at what was done with 0.47.
z-m-08-05.s.s1.r.b: This is a method that lines up the decimal points and subtracts digits in the same places.
z-m-08-05.s.s1.r.c: Changing 3.47 to 3.5 changes the value. Estimating is not a way to find the exact value.
z-m-08-05.s.s1.r.d: This is a method that uses the same denominator and subtracts the numerators.
z-m-08-05.s.s1.r.e: This is a method that splits the subtraction into two steps.
z-m-08-05.s.s1.explain: The methods of Jiho, Raon, and Soyeon all get exactly 6.53 m. Mina did not subtract 0.47 but attached it, so she got 7.47, and Haneul changed 3.47 to 3.5, so she got 6.5, which is not the exact value. Haneul's method can be used for estimating.
z-m-08-05.s.s2.prompt: What is the best reason you can tell, without finishing the calculation, that Mina's answer 7.47 m is wrong?
z-m-08-05.s.s2.hint.0: Compare which is smaller: 10 minus 3, or 10 minus 3.47.
z-m-08-05.s.s2.hint.1: For each choice, tell whether that statement is evidence that 7.47 is wrong or just states a fact.
z-m-08-05.s.s2.o.a: The decimal part of the answer has two digits, so it is strange as a result
z-m-08-05.s.s2.r.a: A two-decimal-place number can be an answer. The number of decimal places is not a basis for judging whether something is wrong.
z-m-08-05.s.s2.o.b: The answer 7.47 is bigger than the number being subtracted, 3.47, so it is strange
z-m-08-05.s.s2.r.b: It is true that 7.47 is bigger than 3.47, but that is not the reason it is wrong.
z-m-08-05.s.s2.o.c: You subtract a number bigger than 3 from 10, but the answer is bigger than 7
z-m-08-05.s.s2.r.c: This is the estimate that since 3.47 is bigger than 3, the length left must be less than 7.
z-m-08-05.s.s2.o.d: An answer with a decimal point cannot be the result of this kind of subtraction
z-m-08-05.s.s2.r.d: In subtraction with decimals, an answer with a decimal point is natural.
z-m-08-05.s.s2.explain: You subtracted 3.47, which is bigger than 3, from 10, so the length left must be less than 7. Mina's 7.47 is bigger than 7, so you can tell it is strange without finishing the calculation.
z-m-08-05.s.s3.prompt: Among the three methods that find the exact answer (Jiho, Raon, Soyeon), choose the one you think suits this calculation best and write your reason. Also add one line about how the numbers would have to change for another method to suit better.
z-m-08-05.s.s3.hint.0: Try the three methods yourself and mark which one is easy to make mistakes in.
z-m-08-05.s.s3.hint.1: Imagine how each method would change if the number subtracted were 3.472 or 3.4.
z-m-08-05.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you check that the method you chose gives exactly 6.53 m?
z-m-08-05.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you think about whether the method you chose would still be useful if the numbers changed (for example, 3.472, or 100 instead of 10)?
z-m-08-05.s.s3.model.0: I find Jiho's column subtraction comfortable. If you write 10 as 10.00, the decimal points line up, so you make fewer mistakes. But if the number is short like 3.4, splitting it into two steps like Soyeon might be faster.
z-m-08-05.s.s3.model.1: Soyeon's method is easy. You subtract 3 from 10 to make 7 and then subtract 0.47, so you can do it in your head. If the numbers are complicated, column subtraction seems safer.

z-m-08-06.title: If you join two ribbons, will they make 4 m?
z-m-08-06.topic: Adding two-decimal-place numbers and units of length
z-m-08-06.goal: Judge whether you can reach a conclusion from the given information, say what else you need to know, and express with numbers how the conclusion changes depending on the conditions.
z-m-08-06.material: To tie once all the way around a box, you need a string of at least 4 m (exactly enough). You have two ribbons: a red ribbon of 2.4 m and a blue ribbon of 1.65 m. You want to join the two ribbons into one. You haven't decided yet whether to join them by 'putting the ends against each other and taping them' or by 'overlapping the ends and gluing them'.
z-m-08-06.thinking.0: Judging whether the information is enough
z-m-08-06.thinking.1: Saying what extra information is needed
z-m-08-06.thinking.2: Expressing with numbers a conclusion that changes depending on conditions
z-m-08-06.prereq.1: Knowing that 1 m = 100 cm and changing units of length
z-m-08-06.s.s1.prompt: With only the information known right now, can we say that this ribbon can tie the box?
z-m-08-06.s.s1.hint.0: Think of the two ways of actually joining the two ribbons, and write down the total length for each.
z-m-08-06.s.s2.prompt: You decided to overlap and glue them. The overlap length can be chosen as a whole number of cm from 1 cm to 8 cm. Write three different overlap lengths x (cm) for which the joined ribbon is still 4 m or more.
z-m-08-06.s.s2.hint.0: Change the lengths of the two ribbons from m to cm and write them side by side.
z-m-08-06.s.s2.hint.1: Change the overlap length 1 cm at a time and check whether the joined length is 400 cm or more.
z-m-08-06.s.s2.ok.c1: The overlap length is a whole number of cm.
z-m-08-06.s.s2.fail.c1: Write the overlap length as a whole number of cm.
z-m-08-06.s.s2.ok.c2: The overlap length is between 1 cm and 8 cm.
z-m-08-06.s.s2.fail.c2: The overlap length must be 1 cm or more and 8 cm or less.
z-m-08-06.s.s2.ok.c3: The joined ribbon is 4 m or more.
z-m-08-06.s.s2.fail.c3: The joined length falls short of 4 m (400 cm). Change the lengths of the two ribbons to cm, add them, then subtract the overlap to check.
z-m-08-06.s.s2.explain: The red ribbon 2.4 m is 240 cm and the blue ribbon 1.65 m is 165 cm, so the sum is 405 cm. To be 400 cm or more after subtracting the overlap, the overlap length must be 5 cm or less. 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5 cm are all possible, and from 6 cm on it falls short of 400 cm. The case with no overlap (0 cm) is also enough, but in this problem you decided to overlap and glue them.
z-m-08-06.s.s3.prompt: When you decide to overlap and glue them, how is it decided whether this ribbon can tie the box? Use the value 4.05 m and connect it with the overlap length in your explanation.
z-m-08-06.s.s3.hint.0: Change the difference between 4.05 m and 4 m to cm and find it.
z-m-08-06.s.s3.hint.1: Write down what happens when the overlap is smaller than that difference and when it is bigger.
z-m-08-06.s.s3.placeholder: e.g., If the overlap is ... or less, then ...
z-m-08-06.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you also write what happens if the overlap is more than 5 cm?
z-m-08-06.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you explain how you found that the difference between 4.05 m and 4 m is 0.05 m (5 cm)?
z-m-08-06.s.s3.model.0: If you overlap and join the ribbons, you have to subtract the overlap length from the sum 4.05 m. 4.05 m is 0.05 m (5 cm) longer than 4 m, so if the overlap is 5 cm or less, 4 m is left and it is enough, and if they overlap by more than 5 cm, it is not enough.
z-m-08-06.s.s3.model.1: If there is no overlap, it is 4.05 m, so it is enough, but if there is an overlap, it is different. 4.05 m − 4 m = 0.05 m, so if the overlap is more than 5 cm, it falls short.

z-m-08-07.title: How many digits does the number made by two cards have?
z-m-08-07.topic: Estimating the size of a product, and the number of digits
z-m-08-07.goal: Test a general claim with counterexamples, estimate the smallest and largest cases, and state the possible range of results together with the conditions.
z-m-08-07.material: Let's make products with number cards. Draw one card with a three-digit number (100 to 999) and one card with a two-digit number (10 to 99), and multiply the two numbers. Minseo said, "When you multiply a three-digit number by a two-digit number, you always get a five-digit number. Because 3 + 2 = 5!"
z-m-08-07.thinking.0: Choosing examples that could be counterexamples
z-m-08-07.thinking.1: Making and checking several cases yourself
z-m-08-07.thinking.2: Estimating the range and drawing a conclusion with conditions
z-m-08-07.prereq.0: Multiplying a three-digit number by a two-digit number by estimating or calculating (Grade 4 level)
z-m-08-07.prereq.1: Counting the digits of a number
z-m-08-07.s.s1.prompt: Choose all the pairs of cards that can be used to show Minseo's statement is wrong. Before calculating, first think by estimating.
z-m-08-07.s.s1.hint.0: For each pair, change the two numbers to the nearest hundred or ten and estimate the size of the product.
z-m-08-07.s.s1.hint.1: Sort the choices by whether the product is less than or more than 10000 (ten thousand).
z-m-08-07.s.s1.r.a: Estimate roughly what the product of the two biggest numbers is. How many digits does this product have?
z-m-08-07.s.s1.r.c: Work out whether 500 × 40 is in the thousands or the ten-thousands. Can this pair shake Minseo's statement?
z-m-08-07.s.s1.r.d: This is the product of the two smallest cards.
z-m-08-07.s.s1.r.e: Estimate whether 120 × 50 is in the thousands or the ten-thousands.
z-m-08-07.s.s1.explain: To shake Minseo's statement, you need a pair whose product is a four-digit number. 345 × 27 = 9315, 100 × 10 = 1000, and 120 × 50 = 6000 are all four-digit numbers. 999 × 99 = 98901 and 500 × 40 = 20000 are five-digit numbers, so they do not contradict Minseo's statement.
z-m-08-07.s.s2.prompt: Test Minseo's statement. Choose a three-digit number a and a two-digit number b to make one pair whose product is a four-digit number and one pair whose product is a five-digit number. (The two pairs must have products with different numbers of digits.)
z-m-08-07.s.s2.hint.0: Start from the small numbers and first count how many digits the product has for numbers like 100 and 10.
z-m-08-07.s.s2.hint.1: Estimate which of a and b you have to make bigger, and by how much, for the product to go over 10000.
z-m-08-07.s.s2.fail.c1: The numbers on the cards are natural numbers.
z-m-08-07.s.s2.fail.c2: a must be a three-digit number from 100 to 999.
z-m-08-07.s.s2.fail.c3: b must be a two-digit number from 10 to 99.
z-m-08-07.s.s2.explain: For example, 345 × 27 = 9315 is a four-digit number and 500 × 40 = 20000 is a five-digit number. 100 × 10 = 1000 and 120 × 50 = 6000 are four-digit numbers, and 999 × 99 = 98901 and 250 × 60 = 15000 are five-digit numbers. It only counts if the two products have different numbers of digits.
z-m-08-07.s.s3.prompt: What can you say about how many digits the product of a three-digit number and a two-digit number has? Write your reason by estimating or calculating the smallest case and the largest case.
z-m-08-07.s.s3.hint.0: Multiply the smallest three-digit number by the smallest two-digit number.
z-m-08-07.s.s3.hint.1: Estimate the product of the two biggest numbers by comparing it with 100 × 100.
z-m-08-07.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you find how many digits the smallest product (100 × 10) and the largest product (999 × 99) each have?
z-m-08-07.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you think about how you can know that every product in between has four or five digits?
z-m-08-07.s.s3.model.0: It is a four-digit number or a five-digit number. The smallest, 100 × 10 = 1000, is a four-digit number, and the largest, 999 × 99, is less than 100000 (one hundred thousand), so it doesn't become a six-digit number. In between, it becomes five digits once it goes over 10000.
z-m-08-07.s.s3.model.1: The product can have 4 digits or 5 digits. 345 × 27 = 9315 has four digits, and 500 × 40 = 20000 has five digits. It can't be less than 1000 and it can't go over one hundred thousand.

z-m-08-08.title: The size of the colored part on a 100-square grid
z-m-08-08.topic: Two-decimal-place numbers seen on a 100-square grid
z-m-08-08.goal: Treat the 100-square grid as 1, write the number of squares as a two-decimal-place number, and make several sizes that fit between two decimals yourself.
z-m-08-08.material: There is a sheet of grid paper with 10 squares across and 10 squares down, 100 squares in all. Say the size of the whole sheet of grid paper is 1. Then one square is 0.01. You color squares on this grid paper with red and blue, using only one color on each square and not coloring over the same square twice.
z-m-08-08.thinking.0: Understanding how the grid and decimals match up
z-m-08-08.thinking.1: Making sizes that meet several conditions at once
z-m-08-08.thinking.2: Explaining a range of sizes using decimals
z-m-08-08.prereq.0: Fractions with denominator 100 and two-decimal-place numbers
z-m-08-08.prereq.1: Comparing the sizes of decimals (Grade 4 level)
z-m-08-08.s.s1.prompt: 25 squares were colored red. Which description of the size of this part is correct?
z-m-08-08.s.s1.hint.0: Using the fact that the whole grid is 100 squares and one row is 10 squares, first write down what part of the whole one row is.
z-m-08-08.s.s1.hint.1: Find out how many squares 0.3 is when written as 0.30, and then compare it with 25 squares.
z-m-08-08.s.s1.o.a: 25 squares is 0.025, because one square is 0.001
z-m-08-08.s.s1.r.a: The whole is 100 squares, so one square is 1 divided by 100. 0.001 is one square when the whole is divided into 1000 squares.
z-m-08-08.s.s1.o.b: 25 squares is 0.25 and it is bigger than 0.3, because 25 is bigger than 3
z-m-08-08.s.s1.r.b: 0.3 can be written as 0.30. Don't compare the digits 25 and 3 as they are; compare the same places.
z-m-08-08.s.s1.o.c: 25 squares is 0.25 and it is smaller than 0.3. 0.3 is 30 squares
z-m-08-08.s.s1.r.c: You changed the one-decimal-place number 0.3 into a two-decimal-place number and connected it to the number of squares.
z-m-08-08.s.s1.r.d: One row (10 squares) is not 1 of the whole but 0.1. The whole is 100 squares.
z-m-08-08.s.s1.explain: The whole is 100 squares, so one square is 0.01 and 25 squares is 0.25. 0.3 is 0.30, which is 30 squares, so 25 squares is smaller than 0.3.
z-m-08-08.s.s2.prompt: Color r red squares and b blue squares. Conditions: color the red part to be bigger than 0.2 and smaller than 0.3, and the blue part to be bigger than 0.05 and smaller than 0.1. Also, the total number of colored squares (r + b) must be odd, and the total must be bigger than 0.3 and smaller than 0.4. Make three different numbers of squares that fit the conditions. (If the total number of colored squares is different, it counts as a different case.)
z-m-08-08.s.s2.hint.0: First write down the range of how many squares you can color red and how many squares you can color blue, each as a number of squares.
z-m-08-08.s.s2.hint.1: Choose one red number and one blue number, add them, and check that the sum is an odd number between 31 and 39 squares.
z-m-08-08.s.s2.ok.c1: The numbers of squares are natural numbers.
z-m-08-08.s.s2.fail.c1: The numbers of squares are natural numbers.
z-m-08-08.s.s2.ok.c2: The red part is bigger than 0.2 and smaller than 0.3.
z-m-08-08.s.s2.fail.c2: The red must be between 21 and 29 squares. 0.2 is 20 squares and 0.3 is 30 squares.
z-m-08-08.s.s2.ok.c3: The blue part is bigger than 0.05 and smaller than 0.1.
z-m-08-08.s.s2.fail.c3: The blue must be between 6 and 9 squares. 0.05 is 5 squares and 0.1 is 10 squares.
z-m-08-08.s.s2.ok.c4: The whole colored part is bigger than 0.3 and smaller than 0.4.
z-m-08-08.s.s2.fail.c4: The total of the red and blue squares is not between 31 and 39 squares.
z-m-08-08.s.s2.ok.c5: The total number of colored squares is odd.
z-m-08-08.s.s2.fail.c5: The total number of squares is not odd.
z-m-08-08.s.s2.explain: (25, 8) is 33 squares, which is 0.33; (22, 9) is 31 squares, which is 0.31; (28, 9) is 37 squares, which is 0.37; and (29, 6) is 35 squares, which is 0.35. The possible totals are four: 31, 33, 35, and 37 squares, and all of them are odd numbers of squares between 0.30 and 0.40 (39 squares cannot be made, because even red 29 squares and blue 9 squares add up to only 38). If you make the same total with different r and b, count it as the same case.
z-m-08-08.s.s2.because.prompt: Choose one of the cases you made, write the total number of colored squares as a decimal, and write why it is bigger than 0.3 and smaller than 0.4.
z-m-08-08.s.s2.because.hint.0: Write the total number of squares you get by adding r and b in the case you chose, and write the decimal you get by dividing that number by 100.
z-m-08-08.s.s2.because.hint.1: Change 0.3 and 0.4 each into a number of squares and compare them side by side.
z-m-08-08.s.s2.because.placeholder: e.g., Red ... squares + blue ... squares = ... squares, so ...
z-m-08-08.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Is the total number of squares in the case you chose really odd and between 31 and 39 squares?
z-m-08-08.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did you change 0.3 and 0.4 into numbers of squares on the grid (30 squares, 40 squares) and compare them?
z-m-08-08.s.s2.because.model.0: Red 25 squares and blue 8 squares make 33 squares, so it is 0.33. 0.3 is 0.30, which is 30 squares, and 0.4 is 40 squares, and 33 squares is between them.
z-m-08-08.s.s2.because.model.1: 28 + 9 = 37 squares, so it is 0.37. 0.37 is bigger than 0.30 and smaller than 0.40. That's because it is more than 30 squares and less than 40 squares.
